analysis.one_liner: Suspends common bee-killing pesticides until the EPA proves they won't harm pollinators.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 75 cosponsors, including one Republican, but never got a vote — it died in the House Agriculture Committee after a single referral to a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to pull from the market the nitro-group neonicotinoid insecticides — chemicals used to coat seeds and spray crops that scientists have linked to mass bee deaths — until the agency completed peer-reviewed field studies showing they cause no unreasonable harm to pollinators. It would also have barred new registrations of those uses in the meantime and directed the Interior Department to monitor native bee populations and report publicly each year. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, then to a subcommittee three weeks later, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and farmers who depend on pollination: the bill's findings cite $24 billion a year in US pollination services and note that one-third of North American food crops — nearly 100 varieties of fruits and vegetables — depend on bee pollination. Commercial beekeepers, who were losing hives at a 45.2 percent annual rate, and growers of bee-pollinated crops would gain if hive losses slowed. Backyard gardeners and native ecosystems would also benefit from lower insecticide levels in soil, water, and wild plants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Beekeepers, fruit and vegetable growers, consumers

how_it_helps.text: It would suspend the registration of imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, dinotafuran, and related nitro-group neonicotinoids for seed, soil, and foliar uses on bee-attractive plants, trees, and cereals until the EPA determines, based on peer-reviewed evidence and a completed field study, that they will not cause unreasonable adverse effects on pollinators. [S2] [S3]
It would block any new EPA registrations for those uses in the meantime, closing the door on new uses being approved while the review is underway. [S2] [S3]

It would require the Interior Department to regularly monitor native bee health, investigate unusual bee die-offs, and publish an annual public report, creating a standing record of pollinator conditions. [S2] [S3]

The bill's findings note beekeepers lost hives at a 45.2 percent annual rate in 2012–2013 and that USDA scientists say losses are too high to guarantee US crops can be pollinated — problems the bill targets directly. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers selling neonicotinoid products and seed companies that sell coated corn, soy, and other crop seeds would lose sales in the US market. Some commodity farmers would face the loss of a low-cost, default seed treatment — though the bill's own findings cite EPA analysis that seed coatings provide little benefit to soybean yields and are unnecessary in roughly 80 to 90 percent of row-crop uses. Farmers who genuinely need the chemicals for a pest outbreak could face higher costs or fewer options.

drawbacks.text: The suspension is not permanent but open-ended: EPA could not lift it until it finished a peer-reviewed evaluation plus a completed field study, which can take years, so farmers relying on these seed treatments would lose access for an uncertain period with no phase-in schedule. [S2] [S3]

Neonicotinoid seed coatings were, by the mid-2010s, the default treatment on most corn and soybean seed; a sudden suspension would force commodity farmers to switch products or untreated seed quickly, and the bill provides no transition assistance or allowance for localized pest emergencies. [S3]

Good-faith objection: critics of blanket bans argue that suspending a whole class of pesticides before field studies conclude is backward — regulating first and studying later — and could push growers toward older, more toxic chemicals if alternatives were unavailable. The bill's standard (proof of no unreasonable adverse effects) places the burden on EPA to complete that science first. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a class of insecticides that the bill's own findings say are unnecessary in most row-crop uses and of little yield benefit, in exchange for protecting pollination services worth $24 billion a year to the US economy. The main honest cost is disruption for commodity farmers who used coated seed as a cheap default and would have had to adjust on the bill's 180-day timeline, plus the possibility that some growers would substitute other chemicals. The trade-off is weighted toward public and agricultural benefit, but the abrupt timeline was a real design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Agriculture Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress: it was referred to a subcommittee three weeks after introduction, never got a hearing or markup, and never came to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Conyers introduced the bill on March 4, 2015, joined by Representative Earl Blumenauer as an original cosponsor. [S1] [S3]

It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture, and on March 23, 2015 to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research — the last action of any kind on the bill. [S5]
The bill finished the Congress with 75 cosponsors, 74 Democrats and 1 Republican. [S4]
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears anywhere in the bill's action history. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neonicotinoid pesticide manufacturers and the seed-treatment business are better off, since the chemicals stayed on the market with no suspension and no new review requirements. The Agriculture Committee's decision not to act preserved the status quo for the entire Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 74 of the 75 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the Republican-controlled Agriculture Committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Neonicotinoid insecticide manufacturers (Bayer, Syngenta, and others)
industries.note: The bill would suspend US registration of their flagship seed-treatment and spray products until EPA proved they were safe for pollinators. Their interest in the bill was keeping those products on the market, which ran directly against the bill's aim of reducing bee mortality.

Most corn and soybean seed was sold pre-coated with neonicotinoids; suspending seed treatments would remove that default revenue stream. The bill's findings cite EPA analysis that the coatings add little to soybean yields, so the lost sales bought consumers and growers little in return.

Beekeepers were losing 45 percent of hives annually and repeatedly losing entire operations; slowing the chemicals most strongly linked to those losses protects their livelihood directly. Their gain — steadier pollination supply — is also the consumer's gain.

They would lose the cheap default seed coating and might face higher costs or fewer options for real pest outbreaks. But the bill's findings cite EPA analysis that the coatings add little to yields in most row-crop uses, so most farmers would lose little of actual value.
